deep.reconstruction:
This page continues Euler's introduction to E283, 'On very large prime numbers', and contains no mathematics in the technical sense.

The argument runs as follows:
(i) The law governing the sequence of primes seems as intractable as squaring the circle. Even so, people who spent effort on it should not be blamed, because any method that overcame the obstacles would be valuable. Primes deserve more attention, since all numbers are built from them.
(ii) Fermat excelled in this field. His proofs were lost after his death.
(iii) Fermat posed to Wallis the problem of exhibiting a prime larger than any given number N.
(iv) Fermat believed he could solve it via the claim that 2^n+1 is prime whenever n is a power of 2. In modern terms, the Fermat numbers F_k = 2^{2^k}+1 would all be prime. Then for any N one could choose k with 2^{2^k} > N, and F_k would be the required prime. Euler stresses that Fermat candidly denied having a proof, though he did not doubt the claim.

The next page completes the thread: Euler recalls his own refutation, 641 | F_5 = 4294967297. He notes that the status of larger F_k is unknown, so the problem stays open. He mentions Euclid's infinitude of primes and his own density remark (the proportion of primes is like log x to x). He then sets up the paper's real aim: finding a formula or method that yields large primes, and testing primality of large numbers.
errors: The historical framing is slightly simplified. Fermat stated the Fermat-number conjecture mainly in letters to Frenicle, Mersenne and Pascal in the 1640s; it reached Wallis via the Digby correspondence (Commercium epistolicum, 1658), where it was posed as a problem to prove. In 1640 Fermat said he lacked a proof. In the 1659 'Relation' to Carcavi he suggested it could be proved by descent. So Euler's statement that Fermat denied having a proof is accurate for the earlier letters but not for all of them.
Saying Fermat's writings were lost overstates the case somewhat. Samuel de Fermat published the Diophantus with observations (1670) and the Varia Opera (1679), but most proofs are indeed missing.
